title: Delica Space Gear
verdict: A second-generation Pajero wearing a people-mover body: Super Select 4WD, a low range and room for eight. It's tall, it leans and its parts take detective work, but nothing else on the import list does family camping on a washed-out logging road quite like it.

paragraphs: On 12 May 1994 Mitsubishi replaced the cab-over [[delica/delica-l300|Delica Star Wagon]] with something that looked like a minivan and drove like a Pajero. The Delica Space Gear moved the engine out from under the driver's seat and into a short nose, sat on the second-generation Pajero platform, and kept a proper 4WD system with high and low range. Japanese magazine Motor-Fan sums it up as a minivan with off-road ability inherited from the Pajero. Thirty years later, that's exactly why North Americans are importing them.

story.heading: A PAJERO UNDERNEATH
paragraphs: Motor-Fan says the fourth-generation Delica was developed on the [[pajero/pajero-gen2|second-generation Pajero]] platform, with a Pajero-derived built-in frame for crash safety and a flat floor from the front seats to the cargo area, so you can walk through the cabin. Wikipedia describes the body as monocoque, unlike the Pajero, with no separate chassis. Underneath it's familiar Pajero hardware: double wishbones and torsion bars at the front, a five-link coil-sprung rear axle, and discs all round, according to the Japanese catalogue data on Gulliver.

At launch the 4WD versions came with a 2.4-litre petrol four, the 3.0-litre 6G72 V6 or the 2.8-litre 4M40 intercooled turbo-diesel. There were rear-drive versions too, with a 2.4, a 2.5 diesel and the V6. Bodies came in standard and long wheelbase, on 2,800 mm and 3,000 mm wheelbases, with an Aero Roof, a High Roof, twin sunroofs or the glass-panelled Crystal Lite Roof. Launch prices were ¥2.408 million for a 2.8 diesel manual and ¥2.80 million for the V6 automatic.

story.heading: SERIES 1, SERIES 2
paragraphs: Japanese catalogue data lists the early 4M40 at 125 PS and 30 kgf·m. From the mid-1997 facelift it's listed at 140 PS and 32 kgf·m, and Wikipedia notes the diesel got an electronically controlled distributor-type injection pump at the same time. The facelift also changed the lights and front panel and replaced the three-section bull bar with a moulded bumper. Owners call these Series 1 and Series 2 vans. Grades ran from XR and XG through Exceed, Super Exceed and Royal Exceed, plus Chamonix and Jasper specials. By mid-1998 the 4WD diesel manual had left the Japanese catalogue.

A final facelift arrived in August 2002, and the catalogue thinned out after it. The rear-drive versions were gone, the 2.8 diesel last appears in the April–October 2004 listings, and the last vans were 3.0 V6 Chamonix and Active Field Edition models with the four-speed automatic. Mitsubishi's Japanese sales were down to 1,451 in fiscal 2006, according to JDMBUYSELL. The catalogue ends in January 2007, when the Outlander-based Delica D:5 arrived with an electronically controlled 4WD system in place of Super Select.

story.heading: THE MONTERO WITH A VAN BODY
paragraphs: The Space Gear was never sold new in North America, but Canada's 15-year import rule let Canadians bring them in long before the US 25-year rule caught up. The Delica Canada forum, much of it based in British Columbia and with threads going back to 2006, has the best advice: tell the parts counter it's a Montero with a van body. One long-time member replaced bearings, seals, brakes, U-joints, CV boots, the pitman arm and ball joints using 1995 Montero parts.

That doesn't always work. Another member bought a Montero head-gasket kit for a V6 Delica and found the head gasket's water passages didn't match. The Drive's 1994 Space Gear owner gives the same advice: cross-reference parts by chassis code, not VIN. In return you get a tall, right-hand-drive, eight-seat van with low range, and the Delica Canada forum is full of owners taking them down gravel and bush roads.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE SPACE GEAR THAT NEVER DIED
callout.title: Starex, Starwagon and a Chinese van that's still in production
paragraphs: Mitsubishi's L400 lived on well beyond Japan. Hyundai used the Delica as the base for the first-generation Starex, built from 1997 to 2007. In Australia the WA-series Starwagon passenger van ran from September 1994 to 2003 and the Express cargo version until 2005. In Taiwan, China Motor Corporation built the Space Gear and gave it its own facelift in 2005.

Wikipedia says Taiwan's Space Gear tooling then went to Dongfeng Liuzhou, whose Fengxing Lingzhi started life as a rebadged Space Gear. Wikipedia lists Chinese production as continuing to the present. In Europe, the passenger version was simply the Mitsubishi Space Gear and the commercial version the L400.

engineering_intro: The Space Gear has a monocoque body with a built-in frame, on running gear taken from the second-generation Pajero. The front suspension is independent, with double wishbones and torsion bars, and there's a five-link coil-sprung live axle at the rear. 4WD versions use Mitsubishi's Super Select transfer case, which lets you choose 2WD, full-time 4WD, locked high range or locked low range. The front axle is engaged by a vacuum actuator.

engineering.note: Pajero-derived structure, flat floor and a walk-through cabin. SWB 2,800 mm and LWB 3,000 mm wheelbases.
Owners adjust ride height with the torsion-bar adjusters, as on a Pajero.
2WD, full-time 4WD, locked 4WD high and locked 4WD low. The front diff is engaged by a vacuum actuator.
125 PS / 30 kgf·m to mid-1997; 140 PS / 32 kgf·m with the electronic pump after that. It has a timing chain.
185 PS / 27 kgf·m all the way through. 2.4 L 4G64 (145 PS) also offered in early 4WD vans.

generations_table.note: Mechanical injection pump. Five-speed manual or four-speed automatic, 4WD.
Electronically controlled pump from the 1997 facelift. Column-shift INVECS-II automatic; the manual leaves the catalogue in 1998.
Four-speed automatic only. The sole engine from late 2004 to the end.
4WD petrol four; rear-drive PA4W versions lasted longer.
Rear-wheel-drive versions. Check the transfer lever before you buy anything sold as a 4x4.
Europe, Australia and other markets. Australia's Starwagon got 2.0 and 2.4 fours and a 3.0 V6.

buying_checks.head: Crawl under it with a flashlight
buying_checks.body: Rust is the van-killer. One Delica Canada owner photographed it on the frame rails, under the battery compartment, in the hole in front of the battery tray, along the seam back to the firewall and behind the rear bumper where the spare sat. Another warned that rebuilding a rotten L400 cost so much time and money he'd never do it again.

buying_checks.head: Look up, too
buying_checks.body: Owners warn about the roof and the windshield surround. Crystal Lite Roof vans are said to be prone to rust and electrical problems, and one owner was quoted about $1,000 for windshield-frame rust repair.

buying_checks.head: Confirm it's actually 4WD
buying_checks.body: Rear-drive Space Gears exist (PA, PB and PC codes). A 4WD van has a Super Select lever and a chassis code such as PD6W, PE8W, PD8W, PF6W or PF8W. Match the code on the frame number to the engine before you pay.

buying_checks.head: Cycle the Super Select
buying_checks.body: Shift through 2H, 4H, 4HLc and 4LLc on loose ground. A front-wheel light that keeps flashing usually means a sticking vacuum solenoid pair or a seized front-diff actuator; a flashing centre-diff light points to the transfer-case position switches.

buying_checks.head: Cold-start a diesel yourself
buying_checks.body: Arrive early so the seller can't pre-warm it. Hard starting points to glow plugs or the glow-plug controller, and smoke can be a clogged EGR, injectors or an injection pump that's on its way out. The early mechanical pump is the one owners say leaks.

buying_checks.head: Check the cooling system and head
buying_checks.body: An owner told Field Mag that overheating and cracked heads are common on L400s. Look for coolant loss, bubbles in the reservoir and white smoke, and ask whether the van has ever overheated. A Delica Canada member advises crack-testing the head if the gasket has gone.

buying_checks.head: Test the automatic properly
buying_checks.body: Drive it until it's warm and make sure it shifts through all four gears. A van that holds third and flashes the neutral light has dropped into limp mode, which can be a sensor fault or a failing transmission.

buying_checks.head: Ask how it got here
buying_checks.body: Get the export certificate, the import paperwork and the build month. In the US the 25-year clock starts at the build date, and RHD insurance and registration rules vary by state and province.

repairs.title: Fix flashing Super Select lights (vacuum solenoids and front actuator)
repairs.cost: Often just cleaning; solenoids and hoses if not
repairs.symptoms: The green front-wheel lights on the Super Select display keep flashing in 2H, or the van won't fully engage or release 4WD. A flashing yellow centre light is a different fault.
repairs.fix: First try backing up a few van lengths and shifting in and out of 4H. Then check the vacuum hoses and the vacuum can at the front diff for cracks or loose hoses. Delica Canada's Big-Bird says the most common cause is the pair of vacuum solenoids behind the engine-bay fuse box: test them for resistance and vacuum hold, and clean or replace them. One owner's dealer fixed it by cleaning a gummed-up solenoid. If the lights still flash, check that the front-diff actuator rod moves freely. A flashing yellow centre-diff light means one of the five shift-position switches on the transfer case is failing.
repairs.tools: Hand vacuum pump · multimeter · vacuum hose · factory manual front-axle section for test values.

repairs.title: Replace the front lower ball joints
repairs.cost: FEBEST joints were about $19 each in 2016, plus shipping
repairs.symptoms: Clunks over bumps, play at the knuckle, torn boots. Lifted vans wear them faster, and Delica Canada members warn that a lift adds strain.
repairs.fix: Support the van on stands, remove the wheel and unload the torsion bar. Separate the lower joint from the knuckle, unbolt it from the lower arm, fit the new joint, then reassemble and get an alignment. Check the part before you start. A member who ordered FEBEST 0420-PD8LLH and 0420-PD8LRH received the flat-bottomed 2WD-type left joint twice from two suppliers. The factory manual shows the 2WD and 4WD joints mounting differently (pages 33A-10 and 33A-11).
repairs.tools: Ball-joint separator · torque wrench · floor jack and stands · factory manual chassis section.

repairs.title: Rebuild the brakes with Montero calipers and pads
repairs.symptoms: Pulling, sticking or seized rear calipers (a common Delica Canada thread), or a failed safety inspection.
repairs.fix: Owners report that 1994–96 Montero front calipers bolt on. One fitted Montero rear calipers to a 2002 L400 and found the brake-line port angled slightly differently, so fit the upper caliper bolt before connecting the hose. Match the hose port on any rebuilt caliper to your old one before you return the core. One owner used Raybestos EHT 530H front pads on a 1995 PE8W. Bleed the system with fresh fluid afterwards.
repairs.tools: Line wrenches · C-clamp or piston tool · bleeder kit · brake fluid.

repairs.title: Replace CV boots (and consider manual hubs)
repairs.cost: Boot kits are cheap; a used axle from an importer if a joint has failed
repairs.symptoms: Grease on the inside of the wheel, a torn or slipped inner boot, clicking at full lock. One Expedition Portal owner had a CV joint break and lose a ball bearing.
repairs.fix: Remove the axle, clean and inspect the joint, and fit new boots, packing grease well up into the ribs (the area most likely to crack, says a Delica Canada member). Lifts increase the axle angle a little, but members say old, dry boots are usually the cause. Manual locking hubs stop the CVs turning in 2WD, which extends their life; the L400 never had them from the factory.
repairs.tools: Axle-nut socket · snap-ring pliers · boot clamp pliers · CV grease.

repairs.title: Clean and check the EGR (4M40)
repairs.symptoms: Black smoke, rough running, carbon build-up in the intake.
repairs.fix: On the Delica Canada forum, one owner calls the EGR valve the first suspect on an imported diesel: it's two bolts and a plate. Another adds that blanking it isn't the first step. Pull the valve, clean the carbon from the valve and its passage, and test the diaphragm with a vacuum tester before you condemn anything. Check the intercooler pipes for oil while you're there; oil in them pointed to failing turbo seals in one owner's 2002 van.
repairs.tools: Sockets · carbon cleaner · scraper · hand vacuum pump · new EGR gaskets.

repairs.title: Fix a leaking 4M40 injection pump
repairs.time: ≈ 6–8 shop hours to remove and refit (one Calgary quote), plus bench time
repairs.cost: Calgary owners were quoted CA$1,600–1,800 in 2016, including removal
repairs.symptoms: Diesel weeping around the pump, hard or rough cold starts, irregular shifting on automatics, smoke.
repairs.fix: Find out which pump you have. Series 1 (to 1997) vans use a mechanical pump, which owners say is prone to leaks but can be resealed and recalibrated in North America. Series 2 vans use an electronically controlled pump, which a shop told one owner no one in North America can calibrate. One owner's rough cold starts and irregular shifting cleared up after a pump overhaul, and a Delica Canada member says a new pump front shaft seal 'does wonders'. Mark the pump timing before removal and have any rebuild bench-calibrated.
repairs.tools: Pump timing tools · sockets and extensions · new seals · diesel specialist for the rebuild.

repairs.title: Head gasket on the 6G72 V6
repairs.cost: Gasket kit plus a timing belt; machine-shop work if the heads are warped
repairs.symptoms: Bubbles in the coolant reservoir, coolant loss, overheating, white smoke.
repairs.fix: Confirm it's the gasket first. Delica Canada members pointed to a YouTube series that walks through the tests before you pull anything. Remove the intake, timing belt and heads, have the heads checked for flatness, and replace the timing belt, tensioner and water pump while it's apart. Buy by part number. One member's Montero (not Montero Sport) kit matched most gaskets, but the head gasket's water passages didn't line up.
repairs.tools: Full metric socket set · torque wrench and angle gauge · cam-holding tools · straightedge and feeler gauges.

repairs.title: Stop the frame rust
repairs.cost: A Fluid Film kit with gun and two gallons came to about CA$230 for one owner
repairs.symptoms: Scaling on the frame rails, rear axle and driveshaft; bubbling around the battery tray and rear bumper.
repairs.fix: Pressure-wash the underside and let it dry for a few days. Take off the side steps and bumper tube to wire-brush and paint the worst spots. A Winnipeg owner says a wire wheel is enough and grinding isn't needed. Then spray an inhibitor into every frame and drain hole, using a wand on a flexible extension. Remove the spare tire first, because one van that was undercoated with the spare left in place rusted behind the rear bumper. Redo it every year.
repairs.tools: Pressure washer · wire wheel · undercoating gun with extension wand · compressor at 70–90 psi · ramps and stands.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: Not much bigger than stock. Japanese 4WD vans came on 225/80R15s, which are about 29 inches, on 15x6 wheels with about 4.25 inches of backspacing. A long-time Delica Canada member says 245/75R16 may fit unlifted, but only with a lot of trimming, and you'll need a lift to clear the wheel wells at full articulation. Even with a 2-inch lift, owners report 31x10.5s rubbing on compression in turns after trimming. One said he should have gone with 30s.

faq.q: Can I import one to the US?
faq.a: Yes, once each van is 25 years old, counted from its build date (49 CFR 591.5). As of October 2026 that covers vans built up to about October 2001: every Series 1 and the early Series 2s. The EPA has a separate 21-year exemption that requires the original configuration. State titling is a separate step, and RHD rules and California smog checks vary. Canada's threshold is 15 years.

Most Space Gears sold on Bring a Trailer in 2025–26 were 4M40 2.8 turbo-diesels, which have a timing chain. Watch it for overheating and injection-pump leaks, and it needs a diesel mechanic. A Delica Canada owner of a long-wheelbase V6 says the 3.0 is quieter with more top-end power, and because the 6G72 was also used in North American Monteros, some engine parts are easier to find. It has a timing belt.

faq.q: What's the difference between Series 1 and Series 2?
faq.a: Series 1 vans (1994 to mid-1997) have the three-section bull-bar front and a mechanical injection pump on the diesel, rated at 125 PS. The 1997 facelift brought new lights, a moulded bumper and an electronically controlled pump, which took the 4M40 to 140 PS. A final facelift followed in August 2002.

The 4WD versions use the Pajero's Super Select system with a two-speed transfer case. You can pick 2WD, full-time 4WD, locked high range or locked low range. Japanese catalogue ground clearance is 190–195 mm (about 7.5 in). It's a monocoque van, though, and Delica Canada members warn that lifted vans used hard can break upper control arms.

faq.q: Why are the Super Select lights flashing?
faq.a: A flashing green front-wheel light usually means the vacuum solenoid pair behind the engine-bay fuse box is sticking, or the front-diff vacuum actuator, can or hoses are faulty. A flashing yellow centre-diff light points to the shift-position switches on the transfer case. Try reversing a few van lengths first.

Ask for parts for a Montero with a van body. Owners have fitted Montero bearings, seals, brakes, U-joints, CV boots, steering parts and ball joints. Match by part number from a genuine catalogue searched by your frame number, because some parts look the same but aren't. Importers also sell used parts, and Delica Canada has a parts trader.

Bad enough to end a van. Owners watch the frame rails, the battery-tray area, the firewall seams, the rear bumper, the roof and the windshield surround. Undercoat as soon as you buy it, and every year after that.

From one owner's manual: 5W-30 or 10W-30 engine oil (4.5 L for the V6, 8.3 L for the diesel), 9.3 L of ATF SP-II M, 2.5 L of 75W-85 GL-4 in the transfer case, GL-5 hypoid oil in the diffs (0.9 L front, 1.6–2.6 L rear), Mitsubishi ATF II in the power steering and about 11 L of coolant.

The common setup is about 2 inches from the torsion-bar adjusters and spacers or stiffer coils at the rear, plus an alignment. Members put a basic kit at about CA$700, plus $400–500 to install. Lift blocks on the ball joints top out around 1.5 inches before camber and tire wear suffer. Heartland in Japan sells 4-, 6- and 8-inch kits that modify the spindles. Expect to replace ball joints more often.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Mitsubishi's 2004 Japanese list rates the 2.8 diesel at 8.2–8.7 km/L (about 19–20 US mpg) in the 10-15 lab cycle, depending on weight. Real-world figures with a tall roof box and all-terrain tires will be lower. The tank holds 75 L (about 20 US gal).

mods.why: Torsion-bar adjustment plus rear spacers or stiffer coils gives about 2 inches; bigger lifts need spindle work. Budget for ball joints and an alignment.
